Missing data

2026-10-16

Source: vignettes/missing.Rmd
missing.Rmd

mcp allows missing values (NA) in the response. This article covers two consequences of that:

  1. Change points in voids: Change points can be inferred in regions with no observed responses.
  2. Imputing missing responses: JAGS treats the missing responses as latent variables and samples them together with the model parameters. You can inspect expected responses with fitted() and the imputation distribution with predict().
library(mcp)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

Inferring change points in voids

Sometimes the interest is not in recovering individual missing responses, but in how gaps in the data affect inference about the change points. To demonstrate this, mcp_example("void") takes the data from mcp_example("demo") and sets the responses near both change points to NA (25 < time < 42 and 70 < time < 80). The top panel shows the fit to the full data and the bottom panel the fit with the voids:

fit_void = mcp_example("void")
## NA values detected in 'response'. JAGS will treat them as latent responses and impute them during sampling.

Notice that mcp can infer change points in regions with no observed data. The first change point joins a plateau to a slope. Its location in the void is mostly informed by extrapolating the two segments until they meet, and the uncertainty is greater than in the full data because fewer data inform these trends. In principle, it could be known to great precision if the segments’ trends were very well defined.

The second change point is different because segment 3 is disjoined from segment 2. There is nothing in the void that tells where the jump happened, so the change point posterior is roughly uniform across the void. This is true for any gap between data: the narrow gap between two neighboring data points (top panel) also yields a uniform-like posterior, just on a much smaller range.

We can quantify how much of each change point posterior is within its void using hypothesis():

hypothesis(fit_void, c(
  "cp_1 > 25 & cp_1 < 42",
  "cp_2 > 70 & cp_2 < 80"
))
## # A tibble: 2 × 7
##   hypothesis             mean    sd lower upper  prob    BF
##   <chr>                 <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
## 1 cp_1 > 25 & cp_1 < 42    NA    NA    NA    NA 0.935    NA
## 2 cp_2 > 70 & cp_2 < 80    NA    NA    NA    NA 0.840    NA

Imputing missing responses

An example with missing responses

The built-in example has a change in slope, a strong difference between two states, scattered missing responses, and a short run of missing responses:

fit = mcp_example("missing")
## NA values detected in 'y'. JAGS will treat them as latent responses and impute them during sampling.

The ordinary plot shows the observed responses and model estimates but omits missing responses. Below, we add them to the plot. These are the rows with missing responses in y:

fit$data |> filter(is.na(y))
##     y  x state
## 1  NA  8     B
## 2  NA 19     A
## 3  NA 27     A
## 4  NA 28     B
## 5  NA 29     A
## 6  NA 30     B
## 7  NA 31     A
## 8  NA 68     B
## 9  NA 84     B
## 10 NA 96     B

Expected responses and predictions

predict() evaluates the posterior predictive distribution at the missing rows, generating fresh simulated responses that include residual variation. The predictions come from trends in non-missing data and what they imply, given the observed covariates (state and x), for the missing rows. Without ar() or ma() terms, as here, these predictions have the same distribution as the JAGS imputations, so we use them as imputations below.

# Mean and 80% posterior predictive interval for missing data
imputed = predict(fit, width = 0.8) |>
  filter(is.na(y))
imputed
## # A tibble: 10 × 7
##        y     x state .mean   .sd .lower .upper
##    <dbl> <int> <fct> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
##  1    NA     8 B      35.5  4.37  29.8    41.0
##  2    NA    19 A      15.4  4.39   9.95   21.1
##  3    NA    27 A      17.1  4.29  11.6    22.6
##  4    NA    28 B      39.3  4.34  33.8    44.9
##  5    NA    29 A      17.5  4.33  12.0    23.0
##  6    NA    30 B      39.9  4.32  34.2    45.3
##  7    NA    31 A      17.8  4.35  12.4    23.4
##  8    NA    68 B      41.3  4.44  35.6    46.9
##  9    NA    84 B      34.6  4.31  29.0    40.1
## 10    NA    96 B      29.5  4.45  23.9    35.2

fitted() has the same syntax as predict() but returns the posterior expected response. Its intervals are narrower because they do not include response variation:

# Mean and 80% posterior interval of the expected response at missing data
fitted(fit, width = 0.8) |>
  filter(is.na(y))
## # A tibble: 10 × 7
##        y     x state .mean   .sd .lower .upper
##    <dbl> <int> <fct> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
##  1    NA     8 B      35.4 1.08    34.0   36.8
##  2    NA    19 A      15.5 0.832   14.4   16.6
##  3    NA    27 A      17.1 0.761   16.1   18.1
##  4    NA    28 B      39.4 0.760   38.4   40.3
##  5    NA    29 A      17.5 0.761   16.5   18.5
##  6    NA    30 B      39.8 0.762   38.8   40.7
##  7    NA    31 A      17.9 0.768   16.9   18.9
##  8    NA    68 B      41.3 1.20    39.8   42.9
##  9    NA    84 B      34.6 0.890   33.4   35.7
## 10    NA    96 B      29.5 1.28    27.9   31.2

Visualizing imputations

Imputations are not added to plot() automatically. Since plot() returns a ggplot, it is easy to extend. Here an × marks the posterior mean and a vertical line shows the central 80% imputation interval:

# Start with mcp plot with prediction interval. Use all draws for less Monte Carlo error.
plot(fit, color_by = "state", interval = "predict", width = 0.8) +

  # Add imputation interval
  geom_linerange(
    data = imputed,
    aes(x = x, ymin = .lower, ymax = .upper),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = "black"
  ) +

  # Add "x" at posterior mean
  geom_point(
    data = imputed,
    aes(x = x, y = .mean),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    shape = 4,  # an "x"
    size = 2
  )

This deliberately distinguishes imputed values from the solid observed points. You can change the interval width, marker, color, or add a subset of the missing rows using ordinary dplyr and ggplot2 code.

The plot above reduces each imputation distribution to an interval. Use summary = FALSE when you need the individual draws instead. Here we plot the imputation distribution for each missing row:

missing_draws = predict(fit, summary = FALSE) |>
  filter(is.na(y))

ggplot(missing_draws, aes(x = .prediction)) +
  geom_density() + 
  facet_wrap(~x)

Probabilistic statements about missing responses

Sometimes, the missing response is of direct interest. For example, you may want to know the probability that a missing response is above a threshold. You can use predict() with summary = FALSE to get all posterior predictive draws and then calculate probabilities of various statements. For example:

missing_draws |>
  filter(.row == 19) |>  # Row number 19 in original data
  summarise(
    p_greater = mean(.prediction > 20),
    p_lower = mean(.prediction < 10),
    p_between = mean(.prediction > 10 & .prediction < 20)
  )
## # A tibble: 1 × 3
##   p_greater p_lower p_between
##       <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl>
## 1     0.146   0.105     0.749

Imputations and other continuous predictors

Plotting differs from fitted() and predict() in one respect: The smooth curves in plot() are evaluated on data made by interpolate_newdata(), which keeps additional continuous predictors (i.e., predictors not assigned an aesthetic) at their observed means by default, or at values supplied through the at-argument. The plot caption reports these fixed values. See the plotting article for using interpolate_newdata() to make your own plots.

The imputation markers above are different: predict(fit) evaluates the original data, so every missing row uses its own predictor values. If another continuous predictor is especially important, an imputation may therefore lie away from a curve drawn at that predictor’s mean. This is expected, just as an observed response with unusual predictor values may lie away from that curve. Use plot(fit, at = ...) or interpolate_newdata(fit, at = ...) or make separate plots when those differences deserve emphasis.

Supported models and limitations

Supported model features

Missing responses work with the usual mcp model features. For example, you can:

  • Include continuous and categorical predictors so imputations follow observed covariate information.
  • Use group-level effects so sparsely observed groups borrow information from the population and their available observations.
  • Model changing residual standard deviation with sigma() so imputation uncertainty can vary over the predictor range.
  • Use binomial, Bernoulli, Poisson, or negative-binomial responses. Their imputations remain on the appropriate discrete response scale; binomial predictions can also be returned as rates.

The predictors required by the model must themselves be observed. mcp currently imputes missing responses, not missing predictor values, and it does not model the process that caused responses to be missing. As with ordinary regression using incomplete outcomes, interpretation relies on the missing responses being reasonably explained by the observed predictors and model structure.

Model evaluation and time series

Missing rows are not treated as observed contributions to log_lik(), loo(), or waic(). For ordinary non-AR/MA models, the remaining observed rows can still be used for these calculations.

AR/MA models need extra care because a missing response can become part of the history for later observations. mcp retains the JAGS draws so fitted() and predict() can reconstruct that history, but it does not currently integrate over missing histories for pointwise likelihood calculations. Consequently, log_lik(), loo(), and waic() are unavailable when a missing response precedes some observed data.

The time-series article discusses this. Use predict(fit, arma = "replicate") or posterior_predict(fit, arma = "replicate") to generate fresh replicated series recursively. Their histories are generated rather than taken from the observed responses. The default predictions condition on observed responses and retained imputations as histories, but still generate fresh outcomes at every row.

Predictions for new data

In AR/MA models, the retained JAGS draws belong to the missing rows in the original fitted data and supply their histories. For the non-AR/MA example in this article, predictions for genuinely new data are ordinary posterior predictions, evaluated just like predictions at the missing rows:

newdata = data.frame(
  x = c(20, 80),
  state = factor(c("A", "B"), levels = levels(fit$data$state))
)

predict(fit, newdata = newdata, width = 0.8)
## # A tibble: 2 × 6
##       x state .mean   .sd .lower .upper
##   <dbl> <fct> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
## 1    20 A      15.8  4.38   10.2   21.3
## 2    80 B      36.3  4.38   30.7   41.8
